title: SoFi Technologies (NASDAQ: SOFI): Building the Bank of the Future — and the Market Just Handed Us the Entry
snippet: Every few years I come across a company that is trying to build something that simply does not exist in Germany yet.
content_html:
Every few years I come across a company that is trying to build something that simply does not exist in Germany yet. SoFi Technologies is one of them. Imagine a single app where you keep your salary account, refinance your student debt, take out your mortgage, buy your ETFs, park your emergency cash at a competitive rate, get your credit card, and even shop for insurance — all under one roof, all mobile, all priced fairly. Everything is fragmented, and the moment you earn a bit more, the incumbents either can’t serve you well or charge you far too much. SoFi has solved exactly this problem in the United States, and its ambition is refreshingly large: to become the primary financial relationship — the Hausbank — for a generation of young, high-earning professionals.

I have wanted to write this piece for a long time. When SoFi came public via SPAC, it was too expensive for my taste and the profitability was still a promise. That promise has now been delivered. The company is GAAP-profitable for the eleventh consecutive quarter, it just posted record Q2 2026 results, and — crucially for a long-term investor — the stock sold off roughly 9% on the print despite an exceptional quarter. That combination, a high-quality compounder marked down on strength, is precisely the setup I look for. On my Fair-PE model I arrive at a fair multiple of 25 and an implied annualized return of about 24%. This is the story of why.

The short version of my thesis: SoFi is a vertically integrated digital bank with its own technology stack, a real banking licence, no branch network, a genuinely beloved brand, and a cross-selling flywheel that has just hit escape velocity. It attacks one of the largest, richest, most inefficient industries on earth — U.S. consumer finance — with a modern brand and a structural cost advantage. It is early, it is still small relative to the incumbents, and the market is currently paying more attention to a single quarter of guidance mechanics than to the durability of a 35%-growth franchise. I think that is a mistake, and I am positioned accordingly.

1. Product, Business Model, Brand and Moat

What SoFi does. SoFi started life refinancing student loans for graduates of top universities — think of it as a modern, digital-native version of what MLP once was in Germany: capture the young academic early, when their income curve is about to bend upward, and grow with them. From that beachhead it expanded relentlessly: personal loans, home loans, credit cards, checking and savings, a brokerage, and third-party insurance. Today SoFi describes itself as the “everything app” for money, and for a growing number of Americans it has become exactly that — the primary place they borrow, save, spend, invest and protect.

How it earns money. There are three engines. First, Lending — personal loans, student loans and home loans — which remains the largest profit contributor and produced record originations of $14.8 billion last quarter. Second, Financial Services — the bank accounts, the card, the brokerage, SoFi Plus subscriptions, interchange — which is where the flywheel lives. Third, the Technology Platform (Galileo and the Technisys core-banking system, now marketed as SoFi Tech Solutions), a genuine B2B business that sells the plumbing — issuing, processing, program management, core banking — to other fintechs, banks and consumer brands. This is the AWS analogy that gets thrown around: SoFi built the rails for itself, learned what a modern financial product actually needs, and now rents those rails to everyone else. Together, fee-based revenue now makes up 39% of the top line — a deliberate, less balance-sheet-intensive, less cyclical mix than a pure lender would carry.

The brand. This is where I get genuinely enthusiastic, because brand in financial services is criminally underrated. SoFi was named the #1 U.S. bank in Forbes’ World’s Best Banks list and took the #1 spot in J.D. Power’s 2026 study for DIY investing. Its unaided brand awareness reached an all-time high of 10% — still low, which to me is upside, not weakness. New customers arrive cheaply through “best-of” placements at the likes of NerdWallet and Bankrate, and increasingly through word of mouth, because — and this is the point incumbents can’t replicate — SoFi can credibly claim to put the customer’s interest first, with cheaper, better products. A bank people actually recommend to their friends is a rare animal.

The moat. SoFi occupies an unusual position: it owns its technology stack, operates with no branch overhead, and holds a national bank charter. That last part matters enormously — it lets SoFi fund loans with its own low-cost deposits (over $45 billion now, more than 90% of its funding base) rather than renting balance sheet from someone else. Pure fintechs have the modern tech but no charter and expensive funding; incumbents have the charter and cheap funding but 1970s technology and branch cost. SoFi is one of the very few players that combines both cost edges at once. Replicating that requires simultaneously building a beloved consumer brand, an owned tech platform, a deposit base and a regulated bank — a decade-long, capital-intensive undertaking. That is a moat.

2. The Market: Enormous, Growing, and Ripe for Disruption

I have a bias, and I’ll own it: I like companies that go after the very largest markets. When the vision is small, most of the upside is already priced in even for a good business. When the vision is Tesla-sized or Netflix-sized and management executes, the achievable market capitalization becomes extraordinary. U.S. consumer finance is one of those markets. Lending, deposits, payments, investing, insurance — the total addressable pools run into the trillions, and the incumbents are fat, slow and still enormously profitable.

That last point is the disruption thesis in a sentence. Just as traditional bricks-and-mortar retail was a soft target for e-commerce, the traditional U.S. bank is a soft target for a digital-native challenger, precisely because it is expensive and still earning very comfortable margins. There is an enormous pool of economics sitting inside legacy institutions that has never been properly contested with a modern brand and modern technology. To frame the runway: JPMorgan is worth well north of half a trillion dollars. SoFi’s market capitalization is roughly $20 billion. This is not a company that has run out of room; it is a company that has barely started, with the ability to keep launching new products into an ever-larger share of each customer’s financial life.

On political risk, U.S. financial services is regulated but stable and rules-based — SoFi navigated the student-loan payment moratorium and a brutal rate cycle without derailing. The genuine sensitivity here is macroeconomic, not political: the lending business is cyclical. If a deep U.S. recession sent credit losses sharply higher, that would hurt. My counter is twofold. First, SoFi deliberately underwrites to a prime, higher-income borrower — people earning six figures who, even in a downturn and even in an AI-disrupted labour market, tend to find work again faster than most. Second, the shift toward fee-based and platform revenue steadily dilutes that cyclicality over time.

3. Culture and Management: Internet DNA Meets Wall Street

Management is a big part of why I trust this one. CEO Anthony Noto is the rare executive who genuinely bridges two worlds. He was a Goldman Sachs partner who ran technology investment banking and helped take Twitter public; he was CFO of the NFL; and he served as COO and CFO of Twitter before taking the helm at SoFi. That combination — deep capital-markets and finance-industry fluency plus authentic internet-and-product DNA — is exactly what you want running a company trying to out-build both banks and fintechs. It also shows in the details: Noto has been a consistent open-market buyer of the stock, which is the kind of alignment I always want to see.

More telling than the résumé is the track record against the plan. SPAC-era projections are notoriously bullish, and most SPAC companies missed theirs by a mile. SoFi did not. It broadly hit its product roadmap and its profitability targets — through a rate-hiking cycle nobody in that original deck had modelled. Delivering GAAP profitability while interest rates were being marched several points higher is, frankly, an underappreciated feat of execution. This is a management team that thinks in years, not quarters, that keeps its promises, and that is building the flywheel patiently rather than chasing vanity metrics.

4. Financials and Margins

The Q2 2026 numbers (quarter ended June 30, 2026) are the best evidence for the thesis:

  • Revenue: record GAAP net revenue of $1.22 billion, up 43% year-over-year (adjusted net revenue $1.21 billion, up 40%). Management raised full-year 2026 adjusted-revenue guidance to $4.75–$4.85 billion and lifted its revenue-growth guide to 32–35%.

  • Members and products: 15.8 million members, up 35%, with a record 1.1 million added in the quarter; products rose 42% to 24.4 million. For the first time ever, SoFi added twice as many products as members — the clearest possible sign the cross-sell engine is working.

  • Cross-buy: 51% of new products were opened by existing members, up from 35% a year ago. Products per member climbed to 1.54. This is the Financial Services Productivity Loop that Noto calls “escape velocity,” and it is the single most important slide in the deck.

  • Lending: record $14.8 billion of originations, up 69% year-over-year — $10.7 billion personal, $2.7 billion student, $1.4 billion home.

On margins, which is where quality gets tested:

  • Net income margin: GAAP net income of $156.6 million on $1.22 billion of revenue is a ~13% net margin — for a company still investing heavily to grow 40%.

  • EBITDA margin: adjusted EBITDA of $357.8 million, up 44%, at a 30% margin. SoFi cleared the Rule of 40 for the 19th consecutive quarter, with a score of 70.

  • Return on equity: tangible book value grew 56% year-over-year to $9.5 billion, or $7.34 per share. Annualized returns on that tangible equity are running in the high single digits today and — this is the key — climbing quarter after quarter as operating leverage kicks in over a largely fixed cost base. That is the pattern I care about most in a scaling bank: once revenue clears the fixed-cost hurdle, incremental economics turn sharply positive.

A note on how I value this business. I am wary of leaning on EBITDA for a bank; for financial institutions I care far more about net interest margin, return on tangible common equity, and the trajectory of book value. On that lens, net interest income rose 52% year-over-year to roughly $790 million, net interest margin held at 5.98%, and the balance sheet is a fortress — a total capital ratio of 18.8% against a 10.5% regulatory minimum, funded overwhelmingly by sticky, low-cost deposits. This company can finance its own growth without tapping the market.

One honest blemish: the Technology Platform segment. It was supposed to be a major growth and profitability driver, and instead it has been the laggard — revenue fell about 23% year-over-year and enabled accounts declined to roughly 135 million, largely because one very large client fully transitioned off the platform. Underlying, like-for-like growth is still positive and new partnerships are landing (Wyndham, Southwest debit rewards, and more brands in the pipeline), but I am not going to pretend this segment has executed to plan. It hasn’t. The offset is that Lending and Financial Services have more than carried the company — which is arguably a better outcome than the original script, since it means the consumer flywheel, not a lumpy B2B pipeline, is doing the heavy lifting.

5. Valuation: A Fair PE of 25 and ~24% Annualized

SoFi guides to full-year 2026 adjusted EPS of around $0.60. At a share price in the mid-$15s, that is roughly 25x this year’s earnings. For a legacy bank that would be absurd; for a business compounding revenue at 35% with expanding margins and a widening moat, it is not remotely demanding — and it is a world away from the pre-profit multiples this stock once carried.

Here is how my Fair-PE (faires KGV) framework handles it. I assign SoFi a fair multiple of 25 — appropriate for a high-quality, founder-caliber-led, platform-and-network-effect franchise with durable 25–30%+ growth, but with a deliberate haircut for the cyclicality of the lending book. I then apply that multiple to my three-year EPS path. If adjusted EPS compounds at roughly 30% from this year’s $0.60 base — conservative for a company this early in its S-curve, and management’s own framework points to at least 30% member growth and durable revenue growth well beyond 2026 — earnings reach around $1.00 within about three years. Twenty-five times that, plus the compounding of a tangible book value already growing north of 50% a year, lands me at an implied return of approximately 24% per annum.

I want to stress the margin of safety embedded in that number, because it is the same logic I applied to my Netflix position. First, the growth estimates I’m using are almost certainly below what a company still adding members at 35% will actually deliver — SoFi has beaten guidance for ten-plus straight quarters. Second, I’m buying below fair value even on nearer-term earnings, so I get paid for the multiple re-rating and the earnings growth and the book-value compounding. Whether I value SoFi as a fast-growing fintech or, more conservatively, simply as a bank on its book value and normalized earnings power, it does not screen as expensive. That is a comfortable place to underwrite from.

6. Risks and Why the Opportunity Exists

So why did a stock this good fall ~9% on a record quarter, sitting closer to its 52-week low of $14.88 than its high of $32.73? Understanding the sell-off is the whole opportunity.

The proximate trigger was guidance mechanics, not fundamentals. SoFi raised its revenue guidance but only reaffirmedits EBITDA and EPS targets, and a handful of analysts wanted the profit guide lifted too. A higher tax rate also clipped EPS by roughly half a cent. The market, as it so often does, decided that a beat which wasn’t a bigger beat was a disappointment. Several banks trimmed price targets by a dollar or two while keeping their ratings largely intact.

The deeper worry investors are chewing on is a narrative one: with 51% of new products now coming from existing members, some read a “shift to cross-buy” as code for “new-member growth is peaking.” I read the same fact as the flagship strength of the model — monetizing a base you already acquired cheaply is the good kind of growth, and member additions were still a quarterly record. There is also the shadow of a March 2026 short report (Muddy Waters) that alleged accounting and charge-off issues; notably, SoFi’s cash revenue has continued to track reported revenue closely, and the credit data has since improved rather than deteriorated.

That is the crux. On the actual credit numbers — the thing bears fear most — personal-loan net charge-offs improved to 3.7%, down 70 basis points sequentially, and 90-day delinquencies fell to 40 basis points. In other words, the market punished the stock on tone and guidance conservatism while the underlying credit and growth held up or got better. The macro backdrop did shift — SoFi now assumes one to two rate hikes in 2026 rather than the cuts it originally penciled in — but it delivered these results into that tougher environment, not away from it.

The genuine, non-narrative risks I do respect: a severe U.S. recession lifting credit losses, continued underperformance of the Technology Platform, and the reality that a lender’s earnings are inherently more cyclical than a pure software company’s. I size the position with that in mind. But “strong company, spooked market, unchanged long-term trajectory” is the textbook definition of where a patient investor wants to be shopping.

7. Latest News and Earnings

The July 29, 2026 print is the headline event, and I’ve covered the numbers above. A few forward-looking items from the call are worth flagging. SoFi Plus, now a paid subscription, has already passed 200,000 paid subscribers at roughly $24 million of annualized revenue — a nascent, high-margin recurring stream layered on top of the bank. SoFi Coach, the AI financial-guidance tool, logged nearly half a million conversations with 90%+ positive feedback, and management is leaning hard into AI both for member engagement and for engineering productivity. The Technology Platform’s reacceleration case rests on new brand partnerships — the Wyndham and Southwest debit-rewards programs, with additional “largest yet” brands signed and awaiting launch. And the capital position (18.8% total capital ratio, self-funded growth) means none of this requires diluting shareholders to finance it.

Net-net: revenue guidance up, profit guidance held, credit improving, capital fortress intact, flywheel accelerating. A very good quarter that the tape chose to sell.

8. Conclusion: The Modern Mobile Bank of America

Strip away the quarter-to-quarter noise and here is what SoFi is: a genuinely high-quality business — rare enough that I don’t find many — with an excellent product, a beloved and still-underpenetrated brand, a structural cost advantage almost nobody else can assemble, a management team that keeps its promises and thinks in decades, and revenue and earnings still growing far faster than a maturing peer set where growth has largely flattened. All of that sits on a strong, self-funding balance sheet, at a valuation that is reasonable on my Fair-PE model and outright cheap on tangible book value.

The bull case, if it plays out, is simple and enormous: SoFi becomes the default primary bank for a generation of Americans — the modern, mobile, everything-app Hausbank — the way Netflix became the default for streaming and Tesla forced an entire industry to follow. When one company credibly targets a market that large and executes, the eventual market capitalization can be a multiple of today’s. Think about the strategic logic even from a competitor’s chair: this is the Mercedes-and-Tesla lesson in reverse. Mercedes held a stake in Tesla and sold it right before it compounded — strategically one of the great unforced errors, because owning even a slice of your most dangerous long-term disruptor would have let you watch the whole thing unfold in comfort. SoFi is that kind of disruptor to the U.S. banking establishment. Owning a position in it is, in part, owning insurance on the future of American finance.

There is also a personal reason this one resonates with me. SoFi’s mission — getting more people to make better financial decisions and giving them fair, low-cost products to do it — is not so different from what I try to do with my own research, my channel, and a cost-efficient fund. I like backing companies whose incentives point the same way as their customers’.

On my numbers, a fair PE of 25 and roughly 24% annualized potential, this is exactly the kind of high-quality compounder-on-sale I want to own for the long run.
